increase.
The Commission cannot raise the final millage above the established in the proposed
millage; however, the final millage rate may be lower than the proposed millage.
A budget workshop is scheduled for Tuesday, August 18, 2026 at 6:00 P.M. in the
Commission Room.

budget for Fiscal Year 2027 are scheduled for Thursday, September 3, 2026 at 6:00
P.M. and Thursday, September 17, 2026 at 6:00 P.M. at City of Cocoa Beach City Hall.
*Rolled-back rate as defined in Florida Statute 200.065 is the millage that provides the same ad valorem tax revenueas was levied during the prior year, exclusive of new construction, additions to structures, deletions, and property
added due to geographic boundary changes.

attachments.name: Cocoa Beach Fire Prevention Code Amendment Ordinance

description:
The proposed amendments are necessary to strengthen the City's ability to enforce compliance with fire prevention requirements, including the payment of required fire inspection fees. Currently, Chapter 9 does not expressly authorize the use of a Notice of Violation (NOV) as an enforcement mechanism, limiting the City's ability to utilize the code enforcement process when fire inspection fees remain unpaid.
The ordinance amends Section 9-6, "Penalties," to include a Notice of Violation as a method of enforcement and updates references to the City's code enforcement provisions. By incorporating NOVs into Chapter 9, the City will be able to refer unpaid fire inspection fees and other fire prevention violations through the established code enforcement process outlined in Chapter 31 of the City Code. This provides a clear administrative pathway to address noncompliance, encourage timely payment of fees, and improve collection efforts while ensuring due process for property owners and businesses.If approved, the ordinance will also amend Section 9-14 to align fire prevention violations and associated civil penalties with the City's code enforcement framework. The amendments will be administered by the Fire Department and Code Compliance staff and will apply citywide. Upon the ordinance becoming effective, staff will be authorized to utilize the Notice of Violation and code enforcement process to address unpaid fire inspection fees and other violations of Chapter 9.
Adopt Ordinance 1722 which updates Chapter 9, "Fire Prevention," of the City Code to improve consistency with the City's code enforcement procedures and clarify available enforcement mechanisms. Specifically, the ordinance amends Section 9-6, "Penalties," to add the issuance of a Notice of Violation (NOV) as an authorized method of enforcement and updates references to the applicable code enforcement chapter. The ordinance also amends Section 9-14, "Classes of Violations and Associated Civil Penalties," to ensure alignment with the enforcement and penalty provisions established in Chapter 31 of the City Code. These amendments provide clearer enforcement authority, improve administrative consistency across City regulations, and support effective compliance with fire prevention requirements.

description:
The City's current solid waste agreement with Waste Management expires on December 31, 2026. Residential single-family customers receiving curbside collection service currently pay $30.70 per month. This rate includes garbage, recycling, and yard waste collection, as well as municipal collection services, with municipal costs bundled into the residential rate at no direct cost to the City.
On March 29, 2026, the City issued RFP CB26-008 Residential & Commercial Solid Waste Services, requesting proposals under two pricing structures. Option 1 separates municipal collection costs from the residential collection rate, with the City paying for municipal services through the General Fund. Option 2 maintains the current pricing structure, with municipal collection costs included in the residential collection rate and no direct cost to the City for standard municipal services.
The Review Committee evaluated the proposals submitted by the two responsive and responsible proposers, Waste Management and Waste Pro, and conducted oral presentations as part of the evaluation process. Based on their evaluations, the Review Committee recommends authorizing staff to negotiate and execute a contract with Waste Management.
Under Waste Management Option 1 (Separate Residential & For-Cost Municipal), residential single-family customers with curbside service would pay $28.83 per month, a reduction of $1.87 per month from the current rate. The City would pay approximately $5,252.24 per month from the General Fund for municipal collection services, with actual costs varying based on the level of service required. This equates to approximately $63,000 a year.
Under Waste Management Option 2 (All-Inclusive Residential & No-Cost Municipal), residential single-family customers with curbside service would pay $30.51 per month, a reduction of $0.19 per month from the current rate. Municipal collection services would continue to be provided at no direct cost to the City, except for any special or additional services requested.
Both options maintain the current garbage, recycling, and yard waste collection schedules while adding weekly routed bulk waste and weekly routed bulk yard waste collection, providing an enhanced level of service and reduced monthly cost for residents.
The Review Committee unanimously recommended negotiating a contract with Waste Management. When considering the proposed pricing structures, the committee voted 3-2 in favor of Option 2 (All-Inclusive Residential & No-Cost Municipal). City Staff requests that the Commission provide guidance on which option to proceed with during negotiations.
title:
Approve the Review Committee's recommendation and authorize staff to negotiate a contract with Waste Management under RFP CB26-008 Residential & Commercial Solid Waste Services. Direct staff to proceed with either option 1 (separate residential & for-cost municipal) or option 2 (all-inclusive residential & no-cost municipal) cost structure.
Staff Representative: Taylor Mottolo, Project Manager
Recommendation: Approve

The evaluation committee has recommended the following 6 companies to aid in the rehabilitation of sewer manholes, mainlines and laterals throughout the City:
Insituform Technologies, LLC

The scope of this Program is to support the City of Cocoa Beach in identifying, evaluating, and rehabilitating components of the sanitary sewer collection system that contribute to inflow and infiltration. Work will be assigned through individual Task Orders and may include manhole rehabilitation, trenchless lining of sewer mains, and the inspection and lining of sewer laterals within designated service areas.
The City of Cocoa Beach will finance this project with funds from the Florida Department of Environmental Protection’s (FDEP) State Revolving Fund (SRF) Special Appropriation for Hurricanes Fiona and Ian (SAHFI). The Contractors will be responsible for completing rehabilitation activities as directed, including coordinating access, preparing work areas, performing cleaning/hauling/disposal and inspection, installing rehabilitation materials, and restoring any disturbed surfaces. Work must be performed in a manner that minimizes impacts on residents, traffic, and surrounding utilities.
Because this is an on‑call contract, specific project locations, quantities, and methods will vary by Task Order. Each Task Order will identify the areas to be addressed, the anticipated scope, and any unique site conditions or requirements. All work shall be completed using industry‑standard practices and in accordance with applicable codes, safety requirements, and City procedures.
Mobilization & DemobilizationMobilization and demobilization will occur for each Task Order issued under this Contract.
Mobilization includes transporting personnel, equipment, tools, materials, and supplies to the designated work area; setting up staging locations, traffic control, and necessary access routes; and coordinating with the City on site conditions and scheduling.
Demobilization includes removing personnel, equipment, temporary facilities, and staging materials; cleaning the work area; and restoring locations disturbed solely due to staging or access.
Mobilization and demobilization will be paid per Task Order in accordance with the applicable unit price schedule.
The Contractor shall submit invoices substantiating the cost of mobilization and demobilization with each pay request. Ten percent (10%) for the cost of mobilization and demobilization will be withheld until acceptance and final payment.
General RequirementsThe Contractor shall maintain required traffic control, coordinate with residents and businesses to maintain reasonable access, protect existing utilities and structures, restore disturbed surfaces, properly haul and dispose of debris and waste materials, and follow all applicable safety requirements, including confined space entry procedures. Contractor to be responsible for necessary water supply required for cleaning activities. City to provide hydrant meters to be paid for by Contractor.
Manhole RehabilitationManhole rehabilitation includes restoring existing sanitary sewer manholes through cleaning, repairs, preparation, and the installation of a lining or coating system. Work may include removing debris or roots; repairing benches, flow channels, and pipe penetrations; addressing active leaks; and correcting localized deterioration that would interfere with rehabilitation or lining.
Following preparation and any necessary repairs, the Contractor will install a rehabilitation lining or coating system as directed by the City. Lining may include applying cementitious or protective materials, reshaping surfaces to acceptable profiles, and completing all steps required to return the manhole to service. Structural modifications may be required where conditions warrant, including adjustments to frames, covers, or internal features.
Mainline Sewer Inspection and RehabilitationMainline sewer rehabilitation generally consists of trenchless lining of existing gravity sewer mains. Work may include cleaning pipelines, conducting pre‑installation CCTV inspection, providing bypass pumping or flow control if necessary, installing and curing a liner suited to existing pipe conditions, reinstating active service laterals, and conducting post‑installation CCTV inspection for verification.
Additional work may be directed by the City, including localized point repairs, excavation and replacement of severely deteriorated pipe, or adjustments at manhole connections.
Sewer Lateral Inspection and LiningLateral inspection work includes locating and inspecting service laterals from the mainline to the cleanout or property boundary and documenting defects or infiltration sources. Based on inspection results, the City may direct the Contractor to line selected laterals.
Lining work may include cleaning and preparation of the lateral, installing a trenchless liner from the mainline connection to the designated endpoint, and performing post‑installation CCTV verification. Work shall be completed in a manner that minimizes disturbance to surrounding property.

description:
Florida Statutes provide for loans to local government agencies to finance the construction of wastewater facilities and Florida Administrative Code requires the formal authorization by the City Commission to formally adopt a facility plan outlining necessary wastewater system improvements to comply with State of Florida funding requirements. Formal adoption of the proposed Facility Plan is required for the City of Cocoa Beach to participate in the Clean Water State Revolving Fund Program.
The Cocoa Beach Water Reclamation Facility Plan Update details recommended improvements for multiple facets of the City’s Water Reclamation Facility (WRF), wastewater collection system, reclaimed water transmission and distribution system, and an inflow and infiltration abatement study and implementation program.
The City of Cocoa Beach was significantly impacted by Hurricanes Fiona, Ian and Tropical Storm Nicole. Sustained, elevated tides and flooded roadways have severely impacted the City’s wastewater collection/transmission systems and wastewater treatment facility. The frequency and severity of extreme weather events have escalated the incidence of sewage overflows. This Plan includes an I&I Abatement Program to reduce inflow, eliminate sewage overflows and illicit discharges.
The recommended improvements can be separated into three projects and are summarized here:
1. WRF Upgradesa. WRF Clarifier Rehabilitation
b. Grit Removal System Evaluation and/or Replacement
c. WRF Generators Replacement
d. Injection Well, Monitoring Wells Cleaning and Inspection/Replacement
e. Reuse Ground Storage Tank Inspection and Repairs
f. Reuse Transfer Pump Evaluation and/or Replacement
g. Drum Screen Replacement
h. WRF Valve Replacements
i. Disc Filter Replacement
2. Inflow and Infiltration Abatement Study and Implementationa. Manhole Inspections, Flow Monitoring, and Smoke Testing
b. Sanitary Sewer Lining
c. Lateral Sewer Lining
d. Manhole Rehabilitation
3. Collection System and Reuse Transmission Improvementsa. Lift Station Upgrades
b. A1A Sewer Crossover Replacement Lift Station #5 Odor Control Project
c. Port Canaveral Sewage Force Main (FM)
d. Patrick Air Force Base (PAFB) Sewage Force Main (FM)
e. Reclaimed Transmission Automated and Manual Valve Replacement
f. Reclaimed Water Distribution System Evaluation

description:
The City’s current Disaster Debris Monitoring Services Agreement with Tetra Tech expires on July 31, 2026. To ensure the continued availability of disaster debris monitoring services, the City issued RFP CB26-010, Disaster Debris Monitoring Services, on May 24, 2026.The selected contractors will provide disaster debris monitoring services and related technical assistance on an as-needed basis. Services include monitoring debris removal, reduction, and lawful disposal activities; documenting contractor operations and debris quantities; supporting compliance with applicable local, state, and federal requirements; and maintaining documentation necessary to support reimbursement of eligible disaster-related costs.
The Review Committee evaluated proposals submitted by two responsive and responsible proposers, DebrisTech and Tetra Tech, in accordance with the evaluation criteria established in the RFP. Based on the evaluation results, the Review Committee unanimously recommends authorizing staff to negotiate and execute contracts with Tetra Tech as the primary contractor and DebrisTech as the secondary contractor.
Establishing primary and secondary contracts provides the City with continuity of services and additional response capacity following a debris-generating event. If the primary contractor is unavailable, unable to meet the City’s required response timeframes, or lacks sufficient capacity to support the City’s needs, the City may activate the secondary contractor to ensure uninterrupted monitoring services and maintain the documentation and oversight necessary to support compliance and reimbursement eligibility.

description:
The City’s current Disaster Debris Removal & Recovery Agreement with Crowder Gulf expires on July 31, 2026. To ensure the continued availability of disaster debris removal and recovery services, the City issued RFP CB26-011, Disaster Debris Removal & Recovery, on May 24, 2026.
The selected contractors will provide emergency debris road clearance (push), disaster debris removal and recovery services to include tree and limb removal, Private Property Debris Removal (PPDR), waterborne debris removal, and Temporary Debris Staging and Reduction Site (TDSRS) management. All work will be performed in accordance with applicable Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), and other federal, state, and local requirements.
The Review Committee evaluated proposals submitted by ten responsive and responsible proposers in accordance with the evaluation criteria established in the RFP. Based on the evaluation results, the Review Committee unanimously recommends authorizing staff to negotiate and execute contracts with five contractors: DRC Emergency Services, SDR, TFR Enterprises, CrowderGulf, and Garner Environmental Services.
Awarding contracts to a pool of qualified contractors provides the City with additional capacity and flexibility to respond to debris-generating events. Because contractor resources may be committed to multiple jurisdictions following a regional or statewide disaster, maintaining multiple pre-event contracts reduces the risk of contractor unavailability and allows the City to activate contractors based on availability, capacity, and the specific needs of the event.

description:
The city's citizen boards (Planning Board and Board of Adjustment) oftentimes sit in a quasi-judicial (QJ) capacity when considering certain application types such as a special exception, or a rezoning. In a QJ hearing, the board acts as a judge, and applies policy as contained in an ordinance to a specific situation.
There are rules and standards set forth in city ordinances regarding criteria that have to be met in order to get a special exception or a variance, what has to be included in a rezoning amendment, and what the standards are for reviewing these applications. The facts of a case are applied to the standards set forth in the ordinance, and the decision must be based on established guidelines and criteria. In a QJ hearing, the board must rely on competent and substantial evidence presented at the hearing. Competent in that the evidence must be from a source that is qualified to speak on the matter, and substantial in that the evidence must provide a reasonable, factual basis for a decision. Decisions cannot be based on speculation, unsupported opinions, or unsubstantiated conjecture.
After a review of the code, staff determined additional QJ criteria are needed and that a uniform set of standards should be developed specifically for city special exception and rezoning requests. To that end, Ordinance 1714 has been prepared to establish these criteria. The criteria will provide a framework to assist citizen boards and commission in evaluating an application to determine if it is consistent with the city's comprehensive plan and land development regulations. Importantly, the criteria will provide the city with legal safeguards, so land use decisions are consistent with applicable state and local law and should a decision be appealed and/or litigated, the city is well positioned to defend itself.
At its April 6, 2026, meeting, the Planning Board unanimously recommended approval of Ordinance 1714 to the city commission.
At its April 16, 2026, meeting, the commission approved the subject ordinance at first reading, with the direction that the draft language be modified to clearly state the board cannot approve a special exception to allow density or height in excess of that allowed in the property's zoning district. The ordinance has been amended accordingly.

description:
With the adoption of ordinances 1542 and 1594, the city established a beach vending program to reasonably permit beach concessions on the ocean beach and to prohibit beach businesses from operating without first obtaining a valid beach agreement from the city. However, it has come to the attention of the city that some people continue unlicensed commercial activity despite repeated citations and prior enforcement actions.
This unlicensed activity interferes with the public's enjoyment of the beach park, inappropriately commercializes the Ocean Beach Park, may obstruct access, burdens city enforcement actions, and undermines the city's carefully regulated licensing system.
To address this, the city attorney has prepared the subject ordinance to address the unauthorized use of commercial equipment on the Ocean Beach Park. The ordinance will authorize city officers (police and code enforcement) to immediately remove and impound the equipment if it is not authorized by a valid beach license. Once impounded, equipment will be stored at a city facility and held until proof of ownership is provided, and city fees and costs are paid. Repeated use of unauthorized equipment may lead to an enhanced administrative hold period not to exceed 12 months, as ordered by the city special magistrate.
At its April 16, 2026, meeting, the commission approved the ordinance at first reading.

description:
On June 23, 2025, the city executed a proposal with Raftelis Financial Consultants, Inc. to complete an impact fee study (Study) for the possible establishment of new police, fire, and public facility impact fees. The completed Study was submitted to the city on January 26, 2026, and is now ready for Commission consideration (Attachment 1).
Background
Impact fees are one-time charges imposed by the city on new development projects. New development places an increased demand on public services. Rather than burden existing residents and property owners with paying for the cost of growth, impact fees aim to ensure that growth pays for itself.
In Florida, local governments have been collecting impact fees since the 1960s. Currently, the city only collects impact fees for wastewater service. This is unusual as the majority of Florida municipalities collect a wide range of impact fees (see Attachment 2 for impact fee survey). This results in a significant loss of potential revenue for the city as well as places the financial burden of new development on residents and property owners. Development in the city will continue to be subject to impact fees imposed by the City of Cocoa (water) and Brevard County (transportation/roads).
The calculation of impact fees involves two main steps:Determining the cost of development-related capital improvements; and
Allocating those costs equitably to various types of development.
Based on the analysis contained in the Study, the impact fee calculation for a single family residence is:Police - $1,080.00
Fire - 1,034.00
General Government - 946.00
TOTAL - $3,060.00
Impact fees for non-residential uses are classified into one of the following four categories and can be found in the Study:Retail/Commercial
Office/Institutional
Hotel/Motel
Industrial/Warehouse.
To limit the financial burden of the proposed impact fees on existing residents and property owners, any development (residential and commercial) that exists at the time of adoption of the proposed ordinance will receive a credit or, in other words, generally be "vested" from the collection of the impact fees for future construction on the property. For example, should a homeowner wish to demolish and rebuild their home, there will be no impact fees collected on the rebuild as the parcel contained a home on the date of ordinance adoption.
The commission approved the subject ordinance on first reading on February 19, 2026. During the City Commission Reports and Announcements portion of the March 5, 2026, meeting, a discussion ensued related to various developments in the city and whether they would be subject to collection of the proposed impact fees. The commission requested the city attorney draft language to exempt projects far enough along in the city approval process from payment of impact required under the proposed ordinance.
A companion resolution will be presented at second reading of Ordinance 1709.
Representatives from Raftelis will be in attendance to provide an overview of the study, as well as answer any questions there may be.

At its January 15, 2025 meeting, the city commission heard public comments regarding the important role of real estate open house signs (a type of temporary sign). Discussion ensued about the need to revise the sign ordinance to allow for more flexible hours for the display of temporary signs in public rights-of-way. At the conclusion of public input and council discussion, staff was directed to place a 30-day moratorium on enforcing the city's sign code provisions related to temporary signs, and to draft code language to address discussed concerns.
In conjunction with the city attorney's office, Ordinance 1711 has been prepared to allow temporary signs to be erected within public rights-of-way between the hours of 10 AM and 4 PM, Saturdays and Sundays. By limiting eligible hours, stated concerns will be addressed, clutter within the rights-of-way will be minimized, and enforcement will be streamlined. The initial draft of Ordinance 1711 allowed for temporary signs up to a maximum of four (4) feet in height, a minimum of five feet from the edge of pavement or face of the curb, and up to three (3) signs per property.
At first reading on February 5, 2026, the commission directed staff to revise Ordinance 1711 to allow for up to five (5) temporary signs per property. All other standards remain the same.

This results in a significant loss of potential revenue for the city as well as places the financial burden of new development on residents and property owners. Development in the city will continue to be subject to impact fees imposed by the City of Cocoa (water) and Brevard County (transportation/roads).
The calculation of impact fees involves two main steps:Determining the cost of development-related capital improvements; and
Allocating those costs equitably to various types of development.
Based on the analysis contained in the Study, the impact fee calculation for a single family residence is:Police - $1,080.00
Fire - 1,034.00
General Government - 946.00
TOTAL - $3,060.00
Impact fees for non-residential uses are classified into one of the following four categories and fee amounts can be found in the Study:Retail/Commercial
Office/Institutional
Hotel/Motel
Industrial/Warehouse.
To limit the financial burden of the proposed impact fees on existing residents and property owners, any development (residential and commercial) that exists at the time of ordinance adoption will receive a credit or, in other words, generally be "vested" from the collection of the impact fees for future construction on the property. For example, should a homeowner wish to demolish and rebuild a home, no impact fees will be collected on the rebuild as the parcel contained a home on the date of ordinance adoption.
Representatives from Raftelis will be in attendance to provide an overview of the study, as well as answer any questions there may be.

They will provide all necessary hardware, software, project management, engineering, programming, graphics, installation, point-to-point startup and, most importantly, staff training and warranty.

description:
The City is authorized to perform a restoration project of a large relic borrow pit within the Banana River through FDEP. The purpose of the project is to eliminate the exposed muck sediments which will result in an overall reduction of Total Nitrogen and Total Phosphorus in the Banana River. The project will entail restoration in the form of placing approximately 265,000 cubic yards (619,8588 square feet) of clean sand over existing muck sediments found within a 140.7-acre area of the Banana River. The clean sand cap placement will vary from 9 inches to 15 inches thick. The authorization also includes the creation of two habitat caps totaling 1.6 acres for oyster and mangrove habitat, upon which 75 black mangrove (Avicennia germinans) seedlings and 350 red mangrove (Rhizophora mangle) seedlings will be planted, totaling 2,700 square-feet (4,500 cubic yards) on the west side of the project area. Those activities include installing a total of 8 low-profile oyster habitat modules, all of which have a 75-foot length and a 10-foot width. Authorized activities are depicted on the attached exhibits.
The City's Permit authorizes 140.7 acres of surface water impacts. Mangroves, wetland vegetation, or submerged grassbeds are not located within the project boundaries; therefore, this permit does not authorize impacts to these resources.
The Site is located within the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) system and is part of the Save Our Indian River Lagoon Program which includes Mosquito Lagoon, Banana River Lagoon, and Indian River (collectively referred to as the Lagoon). Stormwater runoff from urban and agricultural areas, wastewater treatment facility discharges, septic systems, and excess fertilizer applications have led to harmful levels of nutrients and sediments entering the Lagoon. These pollutants have led to muck accumulation within depositional areas of the Lagoon bottom, which flux nutrients, deplete oxygen, and create a bottom that is not hospitable to seagrass, shellfish, or other marine life
The State of Florida and the County have made ongoing efforts to address sources of pollution since the 1970s which have been focused on strengthening source control and discharge regulations. In addition, dredging projects have been ongoing since 1998 to remove muck from the Lagoon and major tributaries, including Crane Creek, Turkey Creek, and St. Sebastian River.
Despite increasing regulations and dredging of select areas within the IRL system, human impacts on the IRL have been occurring for decades resulting in numerous events impacting water quality and marine life. In 2011, an intense algal bloom (referred to as the super bloom) occurred in the Mosquito Lagoon, Banana River Lagoon, and North IRL, as well as a secondary, less intense bloom in Central IRL. The extent and longevity of the super bloom had a detrimental impact on seagrass. There have also been recurring brown tides; unusual mortalities of dolphins, manatees, and shorebirds; and large fish kills due to low dissolved oxygen from
decomposing algae.
As a result, the Save Our Indian River Lagoon Project Plan was developed to outline the numerous target sites listed for further action and their respective contributions to the impacts on the IRL. Additionally, Brevard County taxpayers approved a ½-cent sales tax in 2016 to fund projects intended to reverse IRL water quality declines. The Cocoa Beach Golf Project is the largest project identified in the program with an initial estimated muck area of 140 acres and approximately 1 million cubic yards of muck representing a significant ongoing source of nitrogen and phosphorus flux to the Banana River Lagoon.

description:
The City of Cocoa Beach, like many coastal cities in the State of Florida, is becoming increasingly vulnerable to the effects of sea level rise (SLR), specifically coastal flooding. The City recognizes that both near term and future coastal flooding has direct impacts on residents, business and stakeholders throughout the community. To remain resilient in the face of these inevitable changes, the City of Cocoa Beach has initiated a Vulnerability Assessment (VA) to identify areas under City jurisdiction that are vulnerable to the future impacts of SLR, storm surge, and coastal flooding.
The city is working in partnership with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to ensure the VA follows FDEP’s standard processes to meet the requirements of Florida Statue, 380.093. Successful completion of these requirements will make the City eligible for future grant funding through the FDEP Resilient Florida Program to implement projects to address the impacts of flooding and SLR.
Following FDEP guidelines, a Community Awareness Plan (CAP) has been developed and to outline strategies to inform the public of the VA process and seek input from the community on priority areas where flooding is occurring. Residents and local businesses owners are encouraged to participate in the VA process by completing the survey below, providing input at community engagement workshops, and attending city commission meetings where updates will be discussed.
The VA team will first identify and spatially reference all of the City’s critical assets such as roadways, municipal facilities, and other infrastructure. Thereafter, various SLR, storm surge, and rainfall scenarios will be modeled to assess the vulnerability of critical assets to flooding. Thereafter, adaptation strategies and capital improvement projects will be recommended.
This project is funded through a combination of FDEP grant funding and federal American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funding.
If you are currently experiencing a flooding concern that requires immediate attention, please contact the Stormwater Department via email stormwater@cityofcocoabeach.com.

A review of the current golf rate structure revealed the need to simplify the existing system and adjust fees to better align with operational costs, demand patterns, and regional market rates. At present, the golf course uses a three-season model (Winter, Summer, and Fall) with four separate rate categories in each season: Cocoa Beach Gift Card Program, Cocoa Beach Resident, Florida Resident, and Non-Florida Resident. This structure has become increasingly complex for both customers and staff to navigate.
To improve clarity, consistency, and ease of administration, staff is recommending transitioning to a two-season model (Summer and Winter) with a simplified three-tier rate structure. The proposed categories are:• Cocoa Beach Loyalty Program – available exclusively to Cocoa Beach residents• Brevard County Resident• Non-Brevard County Resident

description:
City staff is aware of recent requests by street performers to use public property. Currently, the city code does not address this activity.
Federal and State law protects freedom of speech and expression, which includes activity such as street performances on public rights-of-way and spaces. However, it is accepted that these expressive activities can be subject to reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions. It is further recognized there is a substantial public purpose in preserving pedestrian and vehicular safety by preventing congestion and obstruction of sidewalks, maintaining safe access to businesses, and preserving aesthetics and quality of life.
For these reasons, the city attorney's office has prepared the subject ordinance. At its core, the ordinance authorizes the creation of specific areas where street performance activities may and may not occur; these are known as "Public Performance Zones" and "Prohibited Areas", respectively.
A companion resolution is being presented in conjunction with first reading of this ordinance to delineate Prohibited Areas. In general, Prohibited Areas are areas in the city subject to congestion and potential conflicts between street performers, businesses, pedestrians and vehicles. Conversely, all other areas not designated as a Prohibited Area is designated as Public Performance Zones, where street performances are permitted.

description:

This pipe was televised in 2024 and upon review we've deemed that it is too risky to line the inside. This pipe has multiple "bellies" where water will sit and become stagnant. The pipe may have shifted or settled within these areas over time causing this issue. We have to clean this pipe almost quarterly to clean any debris that may become entrapped in these bellies so proper flow of water can be achieved. Removal and replacement of this pipe is are only option at this time. Please see attachment for project location.
This area also is home to a pipe along Ocean Beach Boulevard crossing Marion Lane intersection that was discovered to be original cast iron pipe. It's deterioted beyond the point of rehabilitation and removal and replacement is our only option at this time. Please see attachment for project location.
Area two is located at the intersection of St Lucie Lane and S. Banana River Boulevard. There is a section of ductile iron pipe that crosses beneath a 72" concrete storm pipe near the island at this intersection. This section of pipe has become tuberculated over time and creates blockages. This pipe also has to be cleaned on a quarterly basis so proper flow of water can be achieved for this service area. Replacement of this section of pipe is our only option at this time. Please see attachment for project location.
Black & Veatch has been tasked to provide this propsal. B&V is currently assisting the City with two other projects so they are familiar with our needs of the sewer network. Staff is proposing to approve task order #3 for these two new areas as we continue to try and better our sewer utility for our businesses and residents alike.
This is a budgeted capital expense and the full proposal is attached for reference.

The existing City Lift Station #6 is a duplex lift station located on property owned by the City via quit-claim deed from the School Board of Brevard County. The City is seeking to improve the lift station by rehabilitating the lift station by bringing it up to current City standards. Kimley-Horn was tasked with design and engineering to remove the existing valve vault and replace the valve vault piping by bringing the piping assembly above grade with stainless steel piping, replace wet well piping and float system, and request electrical and instrumentation upgrades to the control panel, cabinet and PLC.

description:
City staff is aware of recent requests by street performers to use public property. Currently, the city code does not address this activity.
Federal and State law protects freedom of speech and expression, which includes activity such as street performances on public rights-of-way and spaces. However, it is accepted that these expressive activities can be subject to reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions. It is further recognized there is a substantial public purpose in preserving pedestrian and vehicular safety by preventing congestion and obstruction of sidewalks, maintaining safe access to businesses, and preserving aesthetics and quality of life.
For these reasons, the city attorney's office has prepared the subject ordinance. At its core, the ordinance authorizes the creation of specific areas where street performance activities may and may not occur; these are known as "Public Performance Zones" and "Prohibited Areas", respectively.
A companion resolution is being presented in conjunction with first reading of this ordinance to delineate Prohibited Areas. In general, Prohibited Areas are areas in the city subject to congestion and potential conflicts between street performers, businesses, pedestrians and vehicles. Conversely, all other areas not designated as a Prohibited Area is designated as Public Performance Zones, where street performances are permitted.

description:
Consider Ordinance 1702 on second reading for the regulation of tow truck operations on private parking lots. The current city code is silent on the regulation of towing from private parking lots.
For this reason, staff, in conjunction with the City Attorney, have prepared the proposed ordinance for Commission consideration. The proposed language is partly based on F.S. 715.07, which was amended by the legislature in 2024 to provide additional safeguards for vehicle owners subject to towing. The statute allows municipalities to adopt local regulations above and beyond the regulations contained in the statute. As there have been recent reports in the city of predatory towing companies charging exorbitant fees for removing (and storing) private vehicles from downtown businesses, the proposed language includes:
Requires a tow company to acquire a city permit for non-consent towing from private property in the city
Establishes signage requirements in addition to those promulgated in FS 715.07 to include the placement of a QR on all signage which leads to a website for the tow company where information can be found
Requires a property owner and the tow truck operator to execute a written agreement containing minimum provisions
A tow truck operator shall not begin hooking up a vehicle no less than 15 minutes after he/she has called the police department notifying them of the tow.
Vehicles cannot be towed further than a seven mile radius from the city
Vehicle owners can pay tow fees with check/cash/debit or credit card
A tow truck driver shall take photographs of all sides of the vehicle prior to being towed
As written, Ordinance 1702 will take effect 60 days after its adoption to provide time for the city, property owners, and tow operators to meet the new requirements.
The Commission approved Ordinance 1702 at first reading on August 21, 2025.

The City of Cocoa Beach is considering applying for a grant to the Florida Commerce for a Rebuild Florida Infrastructure Repair Program for Disaster Recovery (DR) from Hurricane Milton, through the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) Community Development Block Grant (CDBG). A total of $400,000,000 is being made available through a competitive application process to local governments located within the forty- seven (47) counties impacted by the 2023 and 2024 Storms. Eligible applicants can submit project applications for a minimum of $750,000 per application.
These funds must be used for potential projects that meet the following threshold criteria:
1. Projects or programs must meet a CDBG-DR National Objective such as:
Benefit to low-moderate-income individuals, Benefit to low-moderate-income areas, and address an urgent need.
2. Projects or programs must meet CDBG-DR Infrastructure Eligible Activities such as:

description:
Emergency Ordinance 1701 has been prepared to provide immediate regulations related to non-consent towing from private property in the city prior to the effective date of Ordinance 1702, which will take effect 60 days after its adoption. Ordinance 1701 takes effect immediately (August 21, 2025).
In general, Ordinance 1701 will require no specific actions by the tow operators other than changing their towing procedures. New signage and permitting requirements are tied to the adoption of Ordinance 1702. Highlights of Ordinance 1701 include:
A tow truck operator shall not connect, tow or remove a vehicle and shall not charge any fee if the owner or person in custody or control of the vehicle returns to the vehicle prior to the tow truck operator having connected the vehicle to the tow truck.
A tow truck operator shall call the non-emergency phone number for the police department and provide the make, model, color, and license plate number of the vehicle to be towed, the location of the planned tow, and the identity of the tow truck driver and tow truck operator. The tow truck driver shall not begin hooking up the vehicle to be towed until no less than fifteen (15) minutes have passed since the phone call with the police department notifying of the tow.
A tow truck operator shall staff or monitor its telephone 24 hours per day and seven days per week, and immediately advise any vehicle owner or authorized representative who calls by telephone prior to arriving at the storage site of the following:
(1) Each and every document or other item which must be produced to retrieve the vehicle;
(2) The exact charges as of the time of the telephone call, and the rate at which charges will accumulate thereafter;
(3) The acceptable method of payment; and,
(4) That the vehicle can be picked up within one (1) hour of request.
Emergency Ordinance 1701 will be repealed upon the effective date of Ordinance 1702.
Resolution 2025-27, which is being presented as a separate agenda item, establishes fines for violations of the emergency ordinance.

description:
Consider Ordinance 1702 on first reading for the regulation of tow truck operations on private parking lots. The current city code is silent on the regulation of towing from private parking lots.
For this reason, staff - in conjunction with the City Attorney - have prepared the proposed ordinance for Commission consideration. The proposed language is partly based on F.S. 715.07, which was amended by the legislature in 2024 to provide additional safeguards for vehicle owners. The statute allows municipalities to adopt local regulations above and beyond the regulations contained in the statute. As there have been recent reports in the city of predatory towing companies charging exorbitant fees for removing (and storing) private vehicles from downtown businesses, the proposed language includes:
Requires a tow company to acquire a city permit for non-consent towing from private property in the city
Establishes signage requirements in addition to those promulgated in FS 715.07 to include the placement of a QR on all signage which leads to a website for the tow company where information can be found
Requires a property owner and the tow truck operator to execute a written agreement containing minimum provisions
A tow truck operator shall not begin hooking up a vehicle no less than 15 minutes after he/she has called the police department notifying them of the tow.
Vehicles cannot be towed further than a seven mile radius from the city
Vehicle owners can pay tow fees with check/cash/debit or credit card
A tow truck driver shall take photographs of all sides of the vehicle prior to being towed
As written, Ordinance 1702 will take effect 60 days after its adoption to provide time for the city, property owners, and tow operators to meet the new requirements.
A resolution to establish towing-related fees associated with Ordinance 1702 will be presented at second reading of the ordinance.

description:
With the adoption of Ordinance 1621 in June 2018, the city established a framework for the regulation of vacation rentals, to include the requirement to register rental units in the RS-1 district as well as establishing maximum occupancy standards. The requirement to register, as well as the maximum occupancy limit, was extended citywide with the adoption of Ordinance 1695 in March 2025.
It has been brought to the city's attention that due to the current definition of "occupant," the number of visitors at a vacation rental can greatly exceed the maximum occupancy allowed by city code. This is because an occupant is defined as an individual staying "overnight" in a vacation rental unit. This has led to large groups/parties gathering at a vacation rental during the day and/or evening that may negatively impact surrounding residences. To address this, the proposed ordinance revises the definition of an "occupant" to include a person who is at the property for more than 15 minutes at any time of the day.
Furthermore, the proposed ordinance exempts infants under two (2) from being considered an occupant. Families occupying vacation rentals oftentimes include children in this age group (infants), and complaints associated with vacation rentals are generally not attributable to infants.
The Commission approved the ordinance on first reading at its June 19, 2025, meeting.

description:
At its May 1, 2025, meeting, the City Commission adopted Resolution No. 2025-09 to enact a moratorium on the enforcement of the city's sign code relating to non-commercial signs. The moratorium is applicable for the period of time beginning sixty (60) days before any election in Brevard County, and ending three (3) days after any such election. The purpose of the moratorium is to provide candidates regulatory relief for election signage until such time as the City Commission considers revisions to its sign code.
Note the resolution continues to prohibit the placement of signs: in rights-of-way/public property/on any utility pole; obstructing the visibility triangle; and signs exceeding 32 square feet on commercially zoned property and six (6) square feet on residentially zoned property.
The Supreme Court, in the Reed vs. Town of Gilbert case, found that government cannot regulate the content of signage; in other words, government cannot treat signs differently based on message. This means the city cannot distinguish (i.e. regulate) between various types of temporary signage, to include election signage, as this would be considered content-based regulation, which is considered unconstitutional.
Currently, the city sign code limits temporary signage on non-residential property to a maximum of nine (9) square feet and shall not exceed two (2) signs per parcel. For residential property, temporary signage shall not exceed six (6) square feet and shall not exceed two (2) signs per parcel. Temporary ground signs cannot exceed four (4) feet in height. These standards do not allow for larger signage (32 square feet) typically used during election cycles.
The proposed ordinance provides that during any gubernatorial, primary, presidential, county or city election year, temporary signage, with property owner consent, may be placed on election day, including 30 days prior to and three days after. During this timeframe, it is proposed that temporary signage not exceed 32 square feet on nonresidentially zoned property and six square feet on residentially zoned property. Furthermore, temporary signage during this period shall not exceed eight (8) feet in height on nonresidentially zoned property, and four (4) feet on residentially zoned property, and any temporary signage over 12 square feet, shall require a city building permit.
All other sign code requirements shall remain in effect.

description:
With the adoption of Ordinance 1621 in June 2018, the city established a framework for the regulation of vacation rentals, to include the requirement to register rental units in the RS-1 district as well as establishing maximum occupancy standards. The requirement to register, as well as the maximum occupancy limit, was extended citywide with the adoption of Ordinance 1695 in March 2025.
It has been brought to the city's attention that due to the current definition of "occupant," the number of visitors at a vacation rental can greatly exceed the maximum occupancy allowed by city code. This is because an occupant is defined as an individual staying "overnight" in a vacation rental unit. This has led to large groups/parties gathering at a vacation rental during the day and/or evening that may negatively impact surrounding residences. To address this, the proposed ordinance revises the definition of an "occupant" to include a person who is at the property for more than 15 minutes at any time of the day.
Furthermore, the proposed ordinance exempts infants under two (2) from being considered an occupant. Families occupying vacation rentals oftentimes include children in this age group (infants), and complaints associated with vacation rentals are generally not attributable to infants.

There is a small area at the end of Cocoa Isles Blvd to install a bioretention area to treat and infiltrate runoff from a low-density residential area. Treatment will be enhanced by lining the retention area with bioactivated media (BAM) and planted with Florida native plants. This system greatly reduces nutrient/pollutant loading to the receiving water while also protecting the barrier island's surficial aquifer. This project will benefit the Banana River Lagoon and this project is being implemented to reduce the pollutant load.
The City is required to meet the Basin Management Action Plan (BMAP) load reductions by 2035. This project will count toward the load reduction needed to meet this requirement.
This proposal consists of engineering, design, permitting, and bidding services.

description:
The City of Cocoa Beach, like many coastal cities in the State of Florida, is becoming increasingly vulnerable to the effects of sea level rise (SLR), specifically coastal flooding. The City recognizes that both near term and future coastal flooding has direct impacts on residents, business and stakeholders throughout the community. To remain resilient in the face of these inevitable changes, the City of Cocoa Beach has initiated a Vulnerability Assessment (VA) to identify areas under City jurisdiction that are vulnerable to the future impacts of SLR, storm surge, and coastal flooding.
The city is working in partnership with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to ensure the VA follows FDEP’s standard processes to meet the requirements of Florida Statue, 380.093. Successful completion of these requirements will make the City eligible for future grant funding through the FDEP Resilient Florida Program to implement projects to address the impacts of flooding and SLR.
Following FDEP guidelines, a Community Awareness Plan (CAP) has been developed and to outline strategies to inform the public of the VA process and seek input from the community on priority areas where flooding is occurring. Residents and local businesses owners are encouraged to participate in the VA process by completing the survey below, providing input at community engagement workshops, and attending city commission meetings where updates will be discussed.
The VA team will first identify and spatially reference all of the City’s critical assets such as roadways, municipal facilities, and other infrastructure. Thereafter, various SLR, storm surge, and rainfall scenarios will be modeled to assess the vulnerability of critical assets to flooding. Thereafter, adaptation strategies and capital improvement projects will be recommended.
This project is funded through a combination of FDEP grant funding and federal American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funding.
If you are currently experiencing a flooding concern that requires immediate attention, please contact the Stormwater Department via email stormwater@cityofcocoabeach.com.

description:
The Wastewater Treatment Facility operates two clarifiers within the biological process of the plant. The biological nutrient removal process consists of two (2) treatment trains each with pre- anoxic, aerobic zones, post anoxic zones, and reaeration. The first aerobic zone has suspended media to promote biofilm growth for increased nitrification. Each treatment train has three (3) individual process trains.
Each process train is served by a circular clarifier. The bottom sludge draw off mechanism was replaced in 2000 with a spiral blade scraper unit. The clarifier drives were replaced during the process conversion in 2012 and perimeter walkways and weir covers were installed. R.A.S. pumps and W.A.S. pumps draw sludge from the central collector. The return and waste activated sludge pumps are new and have variable speed controls.
Along with the clarifier drives, the central collector mechanisms were epoxy coated to prolong the life span. This proposed project is looking to replace the central collector mechanism and upgrade to stainless steel. This project will also consist of weir and launder replacement, and fortifying the weir covers.
The clarifiers operate 24/7 and are crucial to the biological process to separate the settable solids from the water prior to filtration.
This is a much need project for the Wastewater Facility and the project was included in the 2025 Facility Plan making it eligible for SRF Loan reimbursement.
title:

An incomplete application or the non-payment of all related fees shall not be considered to be an application for purposes of determining the date of application. It is noted, that before a vacation rental registration can be completed, such vacation rental must have a current City of Cocoa Beach Business Tax Receipt.

description:
Resolution No. 2025-01 is hereby ratified and affirmed, but it is temporarily revised to provide for a “30-Day Reduced Fee Time Period” (hereinafter “Reduced Fee Time Period”), for the payment of vacation registration fees and late fees. During the Reduced Fee Time Period, the owner of any vacation rental can apply for a vacation rental registration at the reduced fee of $500 per registration of a single vacation rental. At the time of such registration, if there is any late fee associated with that registration, such late fee shall be reduced by 50%. The Reduced Fee Time Period shall begin upon the day after the adoption of Ordinance 1695, which is anticipated to be on March 21, 2025. Therefore, the Reduced Fee Time Period shall begin on March 22, 2025, and end on April 21, 2025 at 4:00 pm. In the event Ordinance No. 1695 is adopted on a date different from March 21, 2025, the City Manager is directed to recompute the determination of the 30 day period for the Reduced Fee Time Period and place those revised dates on the City’s website. To determine the date of application for a vacation rental registration and/or the payment of applicable late fees, (for purposes of determining whether the Reduced Fee Time Period is applicable), the later of the date of on-line or in-person registration and payment of all related fees shall be used. An incomplete application or the non-payment of all related fees shall not be considered to be an application for purposes of determining the date of application. It is noted, that before a vacation rental registration can be completed, such vacation rental must have a current City of Cocoa Beach Business Tax Receipt.
SECTION THREE: Effective Date and Ending Date: This resolution shall become in full force and effect upon final adoption of Ordinance No. 1695, and shall end on that day which is 31 days after the date of final adoption of Ordinance No. 1695.
SECTION FOUR: The City Manager is directed to implement this Resolution and endeavor to publicize the Reduced Fee Time Period in a manner that to the maximum extent reasonably possible encourages the registration of vacation rentals in the City

description:
This project involves upgrade and rehabilitation of Lift Stations 8, 14 and 16. Lift Stations 14 and 16 will convert the existing dry pit, can style lift stations to City standard submersible design.
Lift Station 8 is located on N. Banana River Drive near Jack Drive and borders the City of Cape Canaveral City Limits. We are proposing new valves and stainless steel discharging piping, new control panel, and new fencing around the permitter of the station. If there is room, we are proposing a stand alone permanent generator to be installed and electrical upgrades will be included in the design.
Lift Station 14 is located at 1485 Bayshore Drive. This station serves the Snug Harbor Community in the unincorporated County. This is the original dry pit, can style lift station that was built in 1975. We are proposing to convert the station to a newer standard submersible station and upgrade the electrical system with new control panels.
Lift Station 16 is located at 306 Arthur Avenue. This station serves the North unincorporated County areas. This too is the original dry pit, can style lift station that was built in 1975. We are proposing to convert the station to a newer standard submersible station and upgrade the electrical system with new control panels and install a permanent stand alone generator if there is enough room for one.
The other project on this scope is to evaluate and repair/replace the existing air release valves (ARV's) on the Port Canaveral Sewer Forcemain pipe. The assessment phase will include inspection of approximately 22 ARV's along the pipe run to identify the design and permitting needs and conceptual cost estimate for construction. ARV's play a vital role on pressure forcemains to ensure the entrained air is released to maximize the pumping performance. Entrained air pockets in pipes can cause excessive head loss and flow reductions if not effectively released. This could lead to longer lift station runtimes that put wear and tear on pumps. It could also lead to backups of the lift station if the pumping efficiency is decreased.
Further details are attached with this agenda item.

Every December, the governing body of each member municipality must appoint a Voting Delegate/Director and Alternate to the League.

same time to be a Voting Delegate/Director or Alternate.
Functions: The person appointed as Voting Delegate serves as both the member
municipality’s Voting Delegate at membership meetings and its representative to the
Board of Directors. The Voting Delegate and the Director is the same person. The sole
function of the Alternate for the Voting Delegate/Director is to vote in the absence of the
Voting Delegate/Director.
Following the appointment, the names of the Voting Delegate/Director and the Alternate must be promptly certified in writing to the Executive Director.
Because dues for member municipalities are based on population, each member municipality must also certify its current population figures when it certifies its Voting Delegation/Director and Alternate.
